Mr. Speaker, I cannot understand the reasons which actuate our friends on the other side in apprehending an immediate German peril, and, therefore, insisting upon an immediate contribution to England. But they say, should the peril come, what will you do? And then they quote the words of our noble leader, but not in the way of appreciation, when he said that when that time comes a wave of enthusiasm will traverse this country. Yes, Mr. Speaker, when that time comes. I pray that it may never come; but should it come un-pectedly, in five years, in ten years or next year, that wave of entnusiasm will certainly spread over the whole country, ippeal to the heart of every Canadian, and cause thousands of our young men to go to the assistance of Great Britain. It will rise, Mr. Speaker, to the door of the Canadian treasury, and our patriotic Finance Minister, who thirteen years ago unreservedly gave to the British empire the preferential tariff, will again unreservedly open the doors of the treasury to the British empire according to its need, even if he has in the course of time to convert his surpluses of many millions into as many deficits. But, Mr. Speaker, in time of emergency contributions will be given by whatever governfnent may be in power, though by the expression of hon. gentlemen opposite we would imagine that the present government were to be in power in perpetuity; and it may be that if they are not in power in perpetuity, they may be for a long time. But should the time come when a Conservative government would be in power. I believe a wave of enthusiasm of the Canadian people would then also rise to the doors of the treasury. A contribution, Mr. Speaker, is a matter of a moment. If I understood correctly my hon. friend from St. Anne, he said that contribution does not mean tribute. A contribution for an emergency no doubt does not mean tribute; but if you undertake to-day to help England or the British empire by a contribution, you make it a contribution in the future. It is not a contribution given in a moment of generosity, under special conditions; but when you come to parliament year after year, whether there are good reports or bad reports financially from the country, to have the money voted it certainly becomes a tribute; and under certain conditions, in some particular year, the people of Canada or the members of this parliament might not see the necessity of that tribute, and a difficulty might arise which would not be to the advantage of Canada.
But we are told that a contribution from Canada to-day would give prestige to the British empire. Mr. Speaker, if prestige is required for the British empire, what would give it a greater prestige-a contribution of $25,000,000, of which she has no need, or a contribution of a navy for the protection of trade in this portion of the empire, thus relieving her of the obligation of protecting that trade. We are told that our navy would be of no consideration. It will be of this consideration, Mr. Speaker, that it will have as many ships as England will not require to build for our protection. If every sister nation of the empire can within a few years have a navy sufficient for the protection of its coasts and its trade, England would not be under the necessity of providing for the protection of the commercee of the different nations in her family, and, therefore, would be, like Germany, restricted to the necessity of simnly protecting her harbours and commerce in the North Sea and around the British isles. The interests of Canada and those of the British empire are to-day so closely interwoven that we cannot separate

them. Whatever we do for the development of Canadian resources is for the benefit of England as well as this country; and whatever we do to increase the prestige and the commerce of Great Britain and the maintenance of her supremacy is in the interest of Canada as well as of the other nations of the empire. We cannot separate our interests, and, therefore, we should take no step which might divert the exercise of our energies from the development of our own resourcese of land, forest and sea. WTe should do nothing that would tend to cause a lull in our activity or reduce the revenues of the country, not only in consideration of the material interests of the country, but in consideration of the fact that this development tends to attach more firmly to the country the people of the eastern provinces, and thereby enables us to send more people to develop the provinces of western Canada, where a large proportion of the food of the British empire will be produced in the future. We must never forget, Mr. Speaker, that in the course of a few years-and time travels fast in this twentieth century- Canada may be the only country from which the British isles may obtain foodstuffs, that in the course of perhaps another decade the United States will have no wheat, or a verv small quantity, to export, that in a short time that country will have a population of a hundred million people, and may have to resort to new activities in industry and commerce, and find an outlet for its surplus population. It is already asserted that before the middle of this century, owing to the great activities in the iron industry, the iron deposits of Great Britain may be exhausted, and Canada will then be looked to, to provide the iron and steel for the construction of Dreadnoughts or whatever engines of war will then be required.
One of the greatest duties incumbent on this government is to do all that is possible to promote the development of the iron industry and the iron deposits in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Time we know travels faster now than it ever did. It has travelled faster in the last twenty years than in any previous era, and the day may come shortly when we may be called on to produce and furnish that precious metal for English ships, both in her merchant and naval marine.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Smith) said at that meeting:

Last session at Ottawa he had occasion to refer to military expenditures. He did not complain of their size, but he did complain that the people were not getting all they should from the expenditure. There was not a fair distribution. British Columbia was not getting as fair a distribution as many provinces. He had never been carried away with jingoism.
There again I think the members of this House will recognize the member from Nanaimo.
He had often wondered whether all the fuss that had been made had any foundation. He had met military men, statesmen and others, many experts, and had discussed the situation with them. As a 'democrat' in the old country he had always been against jingoism. His father had told him the Tory party was ever ready with a war scare while the Liberal party was working for the peaceful development of the country. He stated this in explanation. He had, however, listened to the speeches.
And to whose speeches do you think the hon. gentleman had listened?
He had, however, listened to the speeches of Lord Northcliffe, he had read the speeches of Sir Edward Grey, and others,,moderate in tone the most of them, but convincing.
A Crisis at Hand.
After serious consideration he had arrived at the conclusion that there is a crisis in England, and it is necessary for the colonies to interest themeslves in the defence of the empire, it is necessary for them to make their position and interest in the empire felt. He believed that not only was there a crisis but that there was danger, and the time had undoubtedly come when the colonies of the empire should arise and make known their real position.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have read that quotation from the ' Colonist,' which is a Conservative paper in Victoria, but I am glad to be able to say that a representative of the Liberal paper in that city was also present at that meeting. The Minister of Inland Revenue spoke at that meeting also, and as the Minister of Inland Revenue controls the destinies of the Liberal newspaper, the ' Victoria Times, the hon. member for Nanaimo naturally could not expect to have the same amount of space devoted to his speech as the Minister of Inland Revenue had to his, and consequently the *report of the member for Nanaimo's speech in the ' Times ' is not given so fully. However, it was fairly well reported, and from the Victoria ' Times ' of September 25, I quote:
Ralph Smith being called upon, said that he had been commanded by the president of the board of trade to appear. He felt that all the people of British Columbia were in favour of Esquimalt. as a naval base. The imperial authorities had chosen it, and arguments in its favour were superfluous. Every condition
of nature had seemed to have selected it as a suitable place, therefore there is nothing to discuss. The object in asking them to attend the meeting was doubtless that they might give an expression of opinion. Being the member for Esquimalt, from which district he drew so much of his support, it was natural that he would do so. Taking the natural advantages of the place into consideration, and as the member for the district, he would be glad to lend it any support. It was satisfactory to think that Canada had by unanimous resolution of the House of Commons committed themselves to the policy of aiding the defence of the empire. He was glad that they had taken the stand that it was not wise to make a direct contribution, but to build ships of their own.
At the last session of the House he had made a few adverse remarks on the administration of that department, but in discussing the question with men of all lines of thought from the old country he had come to the conclusion that there had arisen a crisis in England, a lid that it was necessary for the colonial interests to make themselves felt.
Here again you recognize the same old story:
His natural tendency was opposed to militarism, but now he believes there was a crisis. Men like Sir Edward Grey and others of the Liberal party who could not he easily led astray by a scare had expressed themselves on this subject, and he was now ready to support any plan for naval defence.
Now, the member for Nanaimo (Mr. Smith) is the gentleman who came into this House two days ago and accused the members on this side of - the House with having changed their views on this question of naval protection. I am sorry the hon. gentleman (Mr. Smith') is not present as I would like to have asked him what is responsible for the change in his views. No change in the meantime has taken place in the conditions to account for his sudden reversion of opinion. We know that, on the authority of the hon. gentleman himself because speaking of the leader of the opposition he said:
There can be no change in any conditions or any circumstances which would correspond to the enormous change in his opinions.
Well, Mr. Speaker, if there was nothing to change the opinion of the leader of the opposition which was expressed twelve months ago, what has happened in the last four months to so diametrically change the opinions of the member for Nanaimo (Mr. Smith). Can it be possible that the hon. gentleman has one opinion on this question for the benefit of his constituents and the people on the Pacific coast, and that he holds another view for the benefit of the right hon. gentleman who leads the Liberal party? I hesitate to think that can be the reason. Is it that he did not fully consider the matter? It cannot be that, because he

told us at the meeting to which I refer that he had come to the conclusion he did come to after serious consideration; and I give the hon. gentleman the credit of giving at least as serious consideration to his remarks in the House as he gave to his remarks made before the public outside of the House. Well, Mr. Speaker, is it the party lash, is it the thumb-screw, to which he has referred? The hon. gentleman, in spite of the fact of his English birth-I think he has enlarged on that once or twice in this House, and 1 am sure that he has done so once at least during this debate-in spite of the fact of His devotion for what he is pleased to call the motherland, and in spite of the. pious affirmation,' an expression which I think has been used before in this debate, he stands in this position, that four months ago he was convinced after serious consideration that there was a crisis in the affairs of the empire, and he is now willing, in obedience to the party lash and the crack of the party whip, to vote for a policy which provides for no immediate aid in that crisis, which in fact negatives immediate aid and provides that there shall be no aid for something like six years. The hon. gentleman said that the party thumb-screw had been applied to me and that I had been compelled to change some of my opinions. Well, I am thankful to say that- if I have experienced the party thumb-screw, although I do not know of it as yet, I certainly have never been placed in as pitiful and humiliating a position as the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Smith) is in to-day.
I would like to refer to one or two little samples of the Consistency and logic of the hon. member, as evidenced by this one speech. I do not propose to go outside of that, because I think it is enough. He scores the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) for what he said concerning British diplomacy. Why, Mr. Sneaker, the feelings of the hon. member for Nanaimo were absolutely hurt. What does he say? He says: 'I myself am a little jealous of Britain and British diplomacy'; and on the strength of that he proceeds to read a lecture to the hon. member for Jacques Cartier. He reads that lecture because that hon. gentleman made some reflections on British diplomacy; but the same hon. member for Nanaimo is prepared to fall in adoration at the feet of the Prime Minister, who said in this House that he hailed with delight the day when Canada would be deprived of the services of British diplomacy. He was quite right to say that he was only a ' little jealous. ' because under the circumstances he can't really be very jealous. Again the hon. gentleman has been one of the strongest advocates of the present policy of the government. In fact, he advocated it so strong-Mr. BARNARD.
ly that he became almost belligerent. He looked and talked like a regular old war-horse. One would imagine he was almost dying to get this navy so that he could go
to war with somebody. What a change has come over the hon. gentleman, if you compare his remarks the other day with those he made when speaking on the budget- last session. These will be found at column 4732 of ' Hansard ' of 1909. Speaking of the expenditures on the militia he said:
I say there is no justification for spending $7,000,000 on the frills and fripperies of militarism. 1 am speaking frankly to the House. I will tell you what I would do with the $7,000,000 that is now expended on the militia. I do not know what it is for. I can quite understand the necessity of defence if you know that there is an existing enemy, but 1 am not aware of any. Where is the possible approaching enemy of Canada ? Where does he live? Do you say in the United States? There never was a time in the history of this country when the feeling between this country and the United States was as friendly as it is at the present time. Where is the eneipy to come from? What are you spending the money for? Is it fashionable to have a militia?
Compare that- language with the language of the hon. gentleman in the House the other day, when he was advocating a naval militia. Is that the language of a man whose heart is sincere for the defence of the country? He went on further to say:
I know it is proper to have a reasonable measure of protection and have it better distributed in Esquimalt as well as Halifax and other points.
What he meant by this is shown by the following remark which he made a little later:
I believe that our coasts should be protected by fishery cruisers and that there should be efficient police supervision and protection along the boundary line. But what I did say and what I repeat is, that a time when you have to restrict the ordinary expenditures of this country in its present state of progress and development, is not the time to expend $7,000,000 of the people's money for military purposes, and that whatever is spent ought to he better distributed to the advantage of the Pacific coast.
This is the last example of the consistency of the hon. gentleman which I pro-' pose to quote. In dealing with his consistency, of which he is so proud, we have found, first, that his opinion of Lord Northcliffe has, for the purposes of this debate, undergone a most radical change; we have found that his careful and seriously considered opinion as to there being a crisis -last September has changed. He was satisfied then that there was a crisis; he is satisfied to-day that there is no crisis. His condemnation of the hon. member for

Jacques Cartier does not, as we say in the west, 'gee' very well with his adoration of the right hon. the Prime Minister. His attitude of militarism last session is very different from is attitude this session. Truly, Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. gentleman spoke with very special knowledge and with great authority when he told this House ' that it was easy to turn around, that it was easy to say one thing to-day and the opposite thing to-morrow.' He made that remark, I think, in a burst of candour, and possibly may be sorry that he said it. He also proceeded to say that it was easy for him to understand the Prime Minister when he said that ' when Britain was at war Canada was at war, and if Britain were at war Canada need not be at war. Mr. Speaker, I do not think the hon. gentleman would have the slightest difficulty in understanding that statement. No gentleman who could so radically change his opinions in so .short a time would have the slightest difficulty in understanding anything his leader might say. If the right hon. gentleman should casually say to him that the moon was made of green cheese, we w'ould have the hon. gentleman standing up in this House prepared to defend the statement at all costs. Now I want to say a word or two in reference to his remarks on a quotation from the speech of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster). He proceeded, by one of his peculiar processes of logic to try and prove out of the mouth of the hon. member from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) that it was quite wrong for Canada to make a contribution of Dreadnoughts at this time. He said:
If I want to find an argument against making a contribution to Great Britain for Dreadnoughts or anything else, I must go to the arguments of these gentlemen a year ago. I take first the argument of the hon. gentleman from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) as hon. members listened to his words, I ask them to keep in mind the policy of the leader of the opposition, and keep in mind also -
This coming from the hon. member for Nanaimo is rather good.
-and keep in mind also the somersault of the hon. member for North Toronto a few days ago in the debate of this Bill-a political somersault that I sumbit, was cleverly executed; no member of the party could execute such an ' about face' as did my hon. friend.
Well, Sir, I venture to say there is a gentleman who comes not very far from Nanaimo who can beat the hon. member for North Toronto as a political acrobat every day in the week. Then he proceeded to say, speaking of the hon. member for North Toronto:
Sneaking of the thing to be considered, he said:
The first is the policy of a fixed annual contribution in money to the British government or the British admiralty. Now, that divides itself, apparently, into two branches, but it is really the same thing. One man says:	Send one million dollars or- two million dollars a year; another man says: Send a Dreadnought or two Dreadnoughts, and so far as Canada is concerned, these two are absolutely one.
Then he continued:
The present policy of the leader of the opposition is to send. Dreadnoughts, but the members for North Toronto demonstrated that, so far as the principle of the thing is concerned, there is absolutely no difference to Canada.
Quoting again from Mr. Foster:
When we translate one contribution into Dreadnoughts it comes down in the end to money which would be sufficient to build and equip a Dreadnought. And, therefore, I say, they are both parts of the one piutusition

The comment of the hon. member for Naniamo on this was:
Now, I would like the hon. member, and especially the hon. gentleman who is to follow me in this debate to remember this.
Again citing from the speech of the hon. member for North Toronto:
-An annual fixed contribution of money to the British government for the purpose of national and imperial defence.
As to this my hon. friend (Mr. Ralph Smith) said:
If that statement he correct, then this House has to consider not only the proposition of the leader of the opposition for two Dreadnoughts at the present time, but the more serious contingency of a repeated contribution to the British empire which is involved in the principle necessarily and according to the hon. member for North Toronto himself.
Now, I wish merely to say this. I am not foolish enough to endeavour to make any defence of the hon. member for North Toronto, for he is quite able to take care of himself; but I do not think it right that he should be misquoted or that his language should go to the public in such a way as to have it misinterpreted. The remarks which my hon. friend from Nanaimo quoted were made, it is true, by the hon. member for North Toronto, taut they were preceded and followed by other statements which gave them a wholly different construction. Before making these remarks quoted by the hon. member for Nanaimo, the hon. member for North Toronto said:
Recollect that my motion deals simply with a stated, regular uniform, normal lines of proceeding and pplicv. Let us argue that out first. It seems to me that when you boil down all the propositions that are made you get down to two propositions, one or the

other of which must in the end he adopted, and I desire for a very few moments to canvass these two propositions, not as an advocate who has dogmatically made up his mind and who admits of no reason on the part of one who takes the opposition thought and might wish the opposition course. But let us, as far as we can, think around them and see what the two mean.
Then came the remarks quoted by my hon. friend. But at the end of his speech the hon. member for North Toronto went on to say:
Outside of any settled action, outside of the normal condition of things in society, in the world, in nationhood, occurences arise, special emergencies, that are unexpected, suddenly loom in view, a great crisis, a great danger. That is absolutely outside of the normal policy to be carried on year after year with settled purposes and upon a settled plan. Every one of the emergencies must be met as it comes and met according to the gravity and importance of the occurence.
Then, winding up bis speech he said:
Let me say to my right hon. friend, that if, after careful consideration, he proposes to this parliament a means for meeting tint emergency adequately by the gift of Dreadnoughts or the gift of money, this side of the House will 6tand beside him in thus vindicating Canada's honour and strengthening the empire's defence.
I do not think that the treatment by my hon. friend from Nanaimo of the speech of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) was fair, nor do I think it was worthy the parliamentary record of my hon. friend. He proceeded after that to run through the statements of a number of the other members of this House, and finally he got down to my humble self and seemed to come to the conclusion that I had said some things on the debate last session which I would now find it necessary to take - back. Well, I have gone over my few remarks on that occasion, and I am happy to be able to tell the hon. gentleman that there is nothing I said on that occasion which I have the slightest desire to withdraw. I began by saying that this government had put the country in a humiliating position. That is a state-' ment which I certainly have no desire to take back. To my mind the result, and the only result of the conference of 1909 was to put Canada still further in a position of humiliation. The only thing shown by that conference was the determination of the government to do just as little as they possibly could. The ministers who went oyer to that conference, showed their determination to shave the proposals of the imperial government just as closely as they could, and at the same time try and preserve some semblance of their own self respect. What has been the course of the government in this whole matter? At the Mr. BARNARD.
1907 conference, we had the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr, Brodeur) taking the glorious position that Canada did not need to do anything for the defence of the empire, because she was protecting her fisheries and had taken over some dockyards. Was not that a glorious position? I am sure that Canada must be proud in having a Minister of Marine and Fisheries who found it necessary to proclaim that we had received from the British admiralty a couple of places in which to store his goods and that he was giving up, one or two cruisers which, so far as our Pacific coast is concerned, were absolutely incapable of doing their work and that he was going to keep up a couple of steamers which were barely sufficient to keep off a few marauding fish thieves. Then we had the Prime Minister's curt refusal to consider, much less discuss, the resolution of Dr. Smartt, of Cape Colony. When we come to the conference of 1909, what do we find? We find that the imperial authorities ask the Canadian representatives for a fleet unit. What was their reply? Well, I fancy that before they gave a reply they put a question, and that question no doubt was, how much will it cost, and I think the answer was not satisfactory. Then the conversation probably went on these lines. They said : * Oh, that is going to cost too much; you have got us over here and now you must help us out; tell us what is the most we can do for the least amount of money, for we have got to go back and bluff these good people of Canada into thinking we are doing something.'
During the recent local by-election in the city of Ottawa, the Minister of Labour (Mr. King) made use of an expression which is possibly more forcible than elegant but which correctly, to my mind very correctly, expresses the situation. He said:
If we act as belly crawlers in the empire we will he treated as belly crawlers and right!v so. If we maintain, our own defences we will he respected by England for it.
It has occurred to me that possibly the Minister of Labour might be in want of an illustration of this particular phrase which he used on that occasion. If he does, I can only point him to the conduct of the representatives of Canada at the imperial defence conference of- 1909.
Now, the proposition of the admiralty was a fleet unit-which meant, of course, as has been pointed out so many times during this debate, a Dreadnought-which should be stationed on the Pacific coast. Well, of course, that would not suit the government. The Secretary of State (Mr. Murphy) at this same meeting at which the Minister of Labour distinguished himself, also made a few remarks.

All this talk about not following the admiralty advice is rubbish. When they talk about the admiralty suggesting a fleet unit they leave out ' on the Pacific.' When the fact that we have two sea-boards to protect- Atlantic as well as Pacific to protect, was pointed out, the suggestion of our ministers was concurred in.
Well, I am satisfied that the admiralty, in making that proposal, were quite well aware that Canada had an Atlantic seaboard as well as a Pacific sea-board. And I think that, in all probability, they were under the impression that the fleet they had on the other side of the Atlantic was quite sufficient for the protection of the Atlantic coast of Canada. At any rate, I am quite sure that they probably remembered-possibly more vividly than did the Secretarv of State-that they had withdrawn forces both from the Pacific and the Atlantic coasts. I think that when it was pointed out to them that Canada's navy must be smaller than originally asked for and then be divided and part placed on the Atlantic and part on the Pacific, it is more likely that thev assented to the division in disgust or in contemptuous indifference. I believe they would have assented equally readily if the representatives of Canada had proposed to put part of the fleet on the coast of Patagonia and part on the Newmarket canal. It certainly is a peculiar argument that because we have a double sea-board, we should reduce the force. We are told that when it was pointed out to the admiralty that, we had two coasts to protect, then it was decided that we would not put the fleet unit on the Pacific coast. So by wav of assisting the empire, our Canadian representatives decided that we would reduce the force and put a little on one coast and a little on the other. Those of us who feel at all keenly on this subject may congratulate ourselves that our representatives forgot that Canada also borders on the Arctic ocean, because, if they had called that to mind, the fleet would have been still further reduced. And if, by any chance, you could twist Hudson bay into a fourth coast, in all probability the Canadian navy would reach the vanishing point altogether. Taking all these matters into consideration. I do not think I want to take back the statement I made last year, that the government had placed Canada in a most humiliating position on this question.
Now it is easy to criticise, but what should these representatives have done? Well, I think that the proper course for them to have adopted was to have placed that fleet unit upon the Pacific coast. That was what the admiralty, who were the best judges of the situation, asked for. Then, if the government had come to the conclusion that it was necessary to defend the Atlantic coast with another fleet unit,
I would have been very glad to support them. If, either because they had plenty of money to spend, or even if they had come to the conclusion that because there happened to be more votes along the Atlantic than along the Pacific coast, they thought the Atlantic coast was the one to be defended, and, if. in taking care of these votes and these voters, they had decided to put a fleet there, as long as they had first put a fleet upon the Pacific coast, I do not think I would have found fault with them, provided always they had made provision for present aid to the empire and for a navy of some efficiency. The Postmaster General (Mr. Le-mieux) in speaking on this question took some pains-speaking mainly, I think, to his friends in the province of Quebec-to let them know about the different countries smaller in population than Canada that have navies (he called them 'colonies'; whether that was a 'slip or not 1 do not know). But, in making that reference, he mentioned such countries as Argentine, Brazil and Chili, countries which we have not been accustomed to think very much superior to our own, and he told his friends how these different countries had navies, but neglected to tell them that any one of these navies built or projected could knock his navy into a cocked hat in five minutes. He was, as I understood him, talking to his friends in the province of Quebec, to make them think that it was their duty, as loyal British subjects, to go in for this little tin-pot navy of his. I do not pretend to know the feeling of the people of the province of Quebec on this subject, but from what I do know of that people, I am satisfied that, if they are prepared to go in for a navy at all, they have enough national pride not to want to build a navy that will be afraid to show itself on a rainy day. The Postmaster General also made a few references to Esquimalt. Without taking up the time of the House too long, -I would like to say a word or two on that subject. The hon. gentleman referred to the taking over of the dockyards at Esquimalt as one more reason why we should have a navy. I do not see the force of what he said about Esquimalt. The Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden) also told us, in the course of his illuminating address, that the reason the cost of the militia had jumped from one and a half millions to seven millions per annum was that he had taken over Esquimalt and Halifax.
Well, Mr. Speaker, when the imperial troops left Esquimalt three years ago they were some 500 strong; to-day the Minister of Militia has the 'magnificent force at Esquimalt of 80 men. The imperial people when in charge of Esquimalt were erecting a new fort; they had spent on what was to be known as the Signal Hill battery, a

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member (Mr. Barnard) who has iust taken his seat will pardon me if I do not follow him in the exact line which he has taken this evening, because his speech seems to be made up more of an attack upon the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Smith) than a discussion of the Bill which is now engaging the attention of this House. As I have no quarrel with the hon. member who has taken his seat, I do not require to take up the cudgels with him. I wish to approach the discussion of the subject before the House with one view and only one view, that which always has been taken by the Liberal party throughout the history of this country-the welfare of our own country and the cultivation of a truly national spirit. I .hope, sir, that no words of mine shall offend even the most sensitive, because I respect the opinions of every hon. member of this House no matter what his politics are, and upon the matter of the merit of the naval Bill I readily understand how different our views may be. It is deplorable to see how members of this House, in the discussion of an important measure such as the one we are now dealing with, should go out of their way to make attacks upon a class of members who may not share their views. I congratulate the hon. member for St. Anne (Mr. Doherty) upon his manly action in repudiating the words which were uttered in this House yesterday. I feel that I must join with him in repudiating the speech, or part of the speech, which was delivered yesterday by one of the hon. members. I have absolutely no mandate to speak for the French Canadians of the province of Quebec, I have not, Sir, a drop of French blood in my veins, but I have no hesitation in saying that if I had I would feel very proud of it, because I know of no class of men in this country who should command the respect of this House more than our French Canadian friends. They have been classed by the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards)-and I want to be perfectly fair with him-as a disloyal body.
May I ask the hon. gentleman if he will quote any words which I have uttered from which he could draw that conclusion.
Oh, yes.
Well do so.

I did not mean to quote the hon. gentleman's speech, but since he has invited me to do so I feel that I will be forced, in answer to his question, to go into th emerits as well as the speech which he has made. When I was a student at college, and it is now a good many years ago
I think I have the hon. gentleman's permission to ask him

Certainly.
Mr. EDWARDS, -if he can state any words I used charging the people of Quebec with being disloyal. I said that I did not use any such words nor any language which could be so construed. My reference was to the leaders of the Liberal party and not to the mass of the people of the province of Quebec, whom I never charged with being disloyal.

I was proceeding, in answer to the question of the hon. gentleman, to say, that when, many years ago, I was a boy at college, I heard an expression used which runs like this:	' Timeo
hominem unius libri ' and I felt, as I listened to the hon. member representing the county of Frontenac, that he was one to whom that expression might be very aptly applied. It was not my intention to go into the merits of his speech, but he invites discussion of it, and I am quite prepared to take up his challenge and discuss it. Let me tell him that he has taken quotations from newspapers in this country that may be adverse to the French Canadian race, he has taken translations which it was proved by the hon. member for St. Anne were not exact, were distorted, he has taken words uttered by one of the greatest French Canadians who ever lived in the province of Quebec, by one whose memory is sacred to the people of that province, a man to whom the province is going to erect a monument, the late Hon. Honore Mercier, he has taken page after page of the same book, and he has argued from these-what? Let me ask him, was he arguing that the French Canadians of the province of Quebec were a loyal people?

I will answer the hon. gentleman since he asks me t)ie question. I was arguing to prove the existence in Quebec, the extent of which I do not know, of an anti-imperial sentiment, due to the teachings of the leaders of the hon. gentleman's own party. As regards the

quotations in the book I am willing to submit that book to which I referred to any gentleman he may name, and I will verify what I said.

I am sorry the hon. gentleman should have invited discussion because I think for his own sake he would have done far better had he allowed his remarks of yesterday to go without having had them put anew upon ' Hansard '. But I will try-and I do it directly against my will in a way-to make it clear to the House that the whole tenor of his speech, or the greater portion of his speech, was designed to show that not only were the French Canadians disloyal, but that hon. members representing constituencies in the province of Quebec were teaching disloyalty to the people of that province. Will the hon. gentleman contradict that?

The hon. gentleman is charging me with saying that the people of the province of Quebec are disloyal. I ask him to either quote those words which he says I used or to withdraw that statement. I did not use any such words, and I ask him either to make good his statement or withdraw his accusation.
I have asked the hon. gentleman a question.
Withdraw, withdraw.

I will read the rule which is as follows:
Whatever a member says in explanation- whether relating to the words or the meaning of his speech-is to be taken as true and not afterwards called into question. The words, which he states liimeslf to have used, are to be considered as the words actually spoken; and the sense in which he says they were uttered, as the sense in which they are to be taken in the debate. If the member disavows the use of words attributed to him, and objected to, the matter must end.

Mr. Speaker, I have the greatest respect for the Chair and I am most ready to obey your ruling. I am also willing to accept the construction which the hon. member has put upon his words, but which I am inclined to think the actual words do not bear out. Now, Sir, I shall proceed to quote from the speech of the hon. member and I only do so in view of the fact that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Edwards) has invited me.
Will you allow me a question? Do you think that all French Canadians to-day are not loyal to the British Crown.
Mr. Speaker, I stated some time ago very clearly and distinctly-
Please answer.
Just sit down.
Continue to read.
I shall do so. You shall get just as much of your speech to-night as you want if you continue interrupting me.
All right.
I continue to quote

Just sit down. I stated very clearly and distinctly that I accepted the position taken last night by the member for Hocbelaga (Mr. Rivet) when he said that the people of the province of Quebec were not disloyal.
The hon. gentleman did not know it untii Mr. Rivet told him so:	.
I have not said one word to charge the mass of the people of the province of Quebec with disloyalty.
Hear, hear.

Oh, that speech is not finished yet.
I have not said anything that could be construed into such a charge. On the contrary, T have said that the people of the province of Quebec have shown a more than ordinary intelligence in resisting the political leaders who for political purposes essayed to lead them from their allegiance, and I do not propose to allow any hon. gentleman from the province of Quebec or from any other province sitting on that side of the House or this to prevert ray language.
Hear, hear.

What did the hon. gentleman mean? He meant that the leaders of political thought in the province of Quebec, irrespective of party, taught disloyalty to the people of the province of Quebec, and these are the words which I object to.
I named the men
They are not all named.
I may have left some of them out. I thought I named enough to satisfy you when I named your leader for one.

Sir Wilfrid Laurier.

The hon. gentleman for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) is going to get into deep water if he begins to name the men whom he charges with disloyalty in the province of Quebec. To-night he mentioned one; he mentioned the name of a statesman who commands the respect of all races and of all creeds throughout this continent when he mentioned the name oi

the Prime Minister. Sir, what is the atti- 1 tude taken by the Conservatives in my native province? Some of the political friends of the hon. member for Frontenac charge the Prime Minister with disloyalty to his race because forsooth according to their statement he is too loyal, and to-night we have the Conservative member for Frontenac charging the venerable leader of this House with disloyalty to the British Crown. Has the hon. gentleman any other leader of the French Canadians to mention? The hon. gentleman does not reply.
I am glad he is not willing to continue the discussion, because the less he says about the disloyalty of the people of the province of Quebec the better for himself. Now, Mr. Speaker, I shall refer to an incident or two in the history of our country, and before doing so, I may state that while 1 have no mandate to speak for the people of Quebec, I have the honour to represent 30,000 of that race, and I want to protest in the name of my constituents, as well as in the name of French Canadians oi Quebec generally, against any charge of disloyalty whether against their leaders- as the hon. member for Frontenac says, irrespective of party-or against the people themselves. I have not allowed political bias to carry me away to such a degree that I would charge any hon. member who does not share my views with disloyalty, but I will say to the hon. member for Frontenac here and now, that the leaders Of political thought in the province of Quebec, from Sir Geogre Etienne Cartiei down to Sir Wilfrid Laurier have been amongst the most loyal men that Canada has ever known. I remind the hon. member for Frontenac that in 1862, Sir John Macdonald having failed to get a Militia Bill through the legislature, it was the French Canadian leader, Sir George Etienne Cartier, who succeeded in that task, thanks to the support he received from his native province, in passing that Militia Bill. This incident is known to every student of history, but I cite it for the instruction of the hon. member (Mr. Edwards), who for the first time learned last night from the hon. member from Hoche-laga that the people of the province of Quebec are a loyal people. Let me say that when Sir George E. Cartier succeeded in carrying that measure, the ' Journal de Quebec,' which was never well disposed towards Cartier praised him for his success in these words:
The Minister of Militia has succeeded where many expected to see him fall. He has nobly retrieved his fortune and has his revenge for his defeat of 1862.
Another French Canadian paper ' La Minerve,' added:
All those present at the sittings of the House during which Mr. Cartier expounded
his militia scheme are unanimous in saying that no other speech of his ever carried more weight or authority, but nothing else could have been expected from the minister who is considered as master of the situation. This is due to the influence derived from his popularity in Lower Canada and to the confidence which his integrity and honesty as a statesman give him in the other provinces.
Let me say further to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Edwards) that if the French Canadian people or at least a large portion of them, are ready to support the government of to-day on a naval policy, it is due to the teaching of the erstwhile leader of the Conservative party, Sir George E. Cartier, and to the teaching of the present leader of the government, another distinguished French Canadian. Sir Wilfrid Laurier. Air. Speaker, let me point out that the French Canadian people do not claim anything out of the ordinary. They have secured certain rights by the treaty of 1763, they have secured certain rights by the Quebec Act of 1774, and they have certain rights which were granted to them by the British North America Act of 1867, upon which our constitution is based. I have yet to hear in the province of Quebec that the French Canadian race are claiming any further rights than those that were given to them by the authority of the British Crown, and those that are given to them by the constitution of their country. Has the hon. member for Frontenac ever inquired whether there might not have been disloyal people from other sources? Does the hon. gentleman remember a speech that was delivered by Sir John Young on his arrival in Canada? Let me quote a passage of it to him. On July 15, 1869, Sir John Young said:
At the present moment Canada is in reality independent. It has its own destinies in its ow-n hands, and its statesmen and people are recognized as competent to judge of then-interests as to what course to pursue to conciliate those interests, England looks to them for her guidance, and whatever then-decision may he, either to continue the present connection or in due time and the maturity of their growth to exchange it for some other form of alliance.
This would be fearfully disloyal language if it were used now by me; but I hope no hon. member of this House will charge me with disloyalty because I repeat the words of Sir John Young. As my hon. friend from Victoria and Haliburton is giving considerable attention to this question of loyalty, I would like for his benefit to read a passage from the ' Times ' of London, which i3 not a French Canadian paper, but the great organ of public, opinion in England.

That seems to me to have been a reasonable sequence of the discussions which have taken place in this House from time to time on this question. What did the iwi- member for North Toronto propose in this House? The wording of his resolution is this:
That in the opinion of this House, in view "f her great and varied resources, of her geographical position and national environments, and of that spirit of self-help and self-respect which alone befits a strong and growing pen-pie, Canada should no longer delay in assuming her proper share of the responsibility and financial burden incident to the suitable protection of her exposed coast line and great seaports.
That was apparently the accepted policy of the Conservative party, and the hon. member for Jacques Cartier did not propose any amendment or offei any objection to such an attitude being taken by this House. Now, Sir, what interpretation could be given to these words which I have just read? Simply the same theory as has been proclaimed from ocean to ocean by His Excellency Earl Grey, the Governor General of Canada. At the risk of being charged with disloyalty, as a member coming from the province of Quebec, I would like to call the attention of the House to some remarks which were made upon this very subject by His Excellency in the city of Quebec on August 22, 1906.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I must call the attention of the hon. gentleman to the fact that to quote or to refer to the Sovereign or his representative with the view of influencing the minds of members is not in order. I will read to the hon. gentlemen the passage:
The use of the name of the Sovereign, or his representative, in debate, so as to interfere with the freedom of disoussion or for the purpose of influencing the determination of the House or the votes of members in respect to any matter pending in parliament, is out of order.
It may be that the hon. gentleman would not seriously think that, but I would prefer that he did not quote His Excellency in this debate.

I was not quoting the Governor General, but Earl Grey in the speeches delivered throughout the length and breadth of this land on this subject.
I could undertsand that the King must not be brought into the discussion of political issues, but if His Excellency, the Governor General, delivers throughout Canada a series of lectures upon imperial questions, I take it for granted that, in so doing, he' is

not speaking as the Governor General of Canada, but simply as Earl Grey, and it was simply the words of Earl Grey, that I meant to quote. But of course, Sir, if you rule that I am not to quote any language uttered by Earl Grey
I think it would be better that the hon. gentleman should not. I cannot discriminate between Earl Grey and the Governor General at the present time. The rule is explicit enough.
I bow to your ruling, Sir. I had no desire to be discourteous to the Governor General, and shall, in obedience to your ruling, pass over what His Excellency has said.

I do not think the hon. gentleman has been understood as being in any sense discourteous, but simply as not being in accord with the rule of the House, which forbids any expressions of opinion by the Governor General to be used in debate.

It is not a question of discourtesy at all. The rule is that no reference may be made to the representative of the Sovereign for the purpose of influencing the votes or opinions of members in this House.

I must say that even the statement made by the hon. gentleman
implying that the Governor General sent him this pamphlet would m itself naturally provoke discussion if went on with, and would lead to irregularity in the debate whijh it is very desirable to avoid.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, to your ruling.

Without questioning your ruling, Mr. Speaker, I may say that His Excellency drew a distinction in the speeches delivered in the Northwest, in which he said he spoke as Earl Grey, but not as the Governor General.
I do not know what the article is, but I presume it is complimentary to His Excellency, but is it not better to keep all this thing out of debate and observe the rule?

I submit to your ruling, Mr. Speaker, and, the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Hughes) says, it may be just as well to keep His Excellency out of the debate; but as most of the eminent men of the United Kingdom have been quoted, I thought it would not be derogatory to the dignity of His Excellency to give his opinion also.
After the hon. member lor North Toronto (Mr. Foster) offered his resolution, the government proposed another resolution which was in the nature of the policy this government intended to adopt. That resolution read as follows:
The House fully recognizes the duty of the people of Canada, as they increase in numbers and wealth, to assume in larger measure the responsibilities of national defence.
The House is of opinion that under the present constitutional relations between the mother country and the self-governing dominions, the payment of regular and periodical contributions to the imperial treasury.
I would like to call the attention of hon. gentlemen opposite to those words:
For naval and military purposes would not, so far as Canada is concerned, be the most satisfactory solution of the question of defence.
The House will cordially approve of any necessary expenditure designed to promote the speedy organization of a Canadian naval service in co-operation with and in close relation to the imperial navy, along the lines suggested by the admiralty at the last imperial conference, and in full sympathy with the view that the naval supremacy of Britain is essential to the security of commerce, the safety of the empire and the peace of the world.
The House expresses its firm conviction that whenever the need arises the Canadian people will be found ready and willing to make any sacrifice that is required to give to the imperial authorities the most loyal and hearty co-operation in every movement for the maintenance of the integrity and honour of the empire.

The hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) did not at that moment offer any objection or give notice of any amendment, and the resolution was adopted unanimously and declared to be the policy of this country, and that resolution is in conformity with the Bill we are now considering. I submit that, no matter what may have been the differences of opinion as to the advisability of the introduction of such a resolution, once it had been passed, and passed unanimously, there was no alternative for the government, but to bring down the Bill they did. Let me say that the building of a navy for Canada, as one of the great nations within the British empire, imposes itself as a necessity upon the Canadian people. Our population is increasing, our resources are being developed, Canada is gradually growing into nationhood, our exports are increasing beyond the dreams of the Canada of a few years ago. We have been invited, time and again, to do our share towards upholding the strength of the British empire. We have been invited to contribute towards the British navy. We have been invited to build our own ships. And, in the consideration of the different proposals which were before this country, Canada adopted the course which, to my mind, was the wisest, that of building a navy of her own.
Let me say a word about the criticism that is offered to that navy as a navy. The hon. member for St. Anne, Montreal (Mr. Doherty)-and I will not criticise his speech at all-spoke of a navy as a means of attack, and not as a means of defence. Well, Sir, that is a pretty fine distinction to draw. A navy may be a means of attack if attack is necessary, but always a means of defence. Now, not only that but he and other hon. gentlemen opposite have criticised the advisability of bpilding what they have termed ' this small flotilla '. I am unfortunately, not a naval expert, and I have been forced to go to authorities for information upon navy matters. In the course of reading the expressions at the several conferences, I came upon this word, uttered by Lord Tweedmouth, the First Lord of the Admiralty:
There is, I think, a further advantage in these small flotillas, that they will be an admirable means of coast defence.
Sir, I take_ the opinion of the First Lord of the Admiralty as against the opinion of hon. gentlemen opposite. And if the First Lord of the Admiralty tells the representatives of our country in London, and tells this parliament, through the conference, that what this government proposes to build in the way of a navy, this ' flotilla ' that the government proptoses to build, would be a sure means of defence of our shores, then, Sir, I think we have lived up to that portion of the resolution Mr. DEVLIN.
which was introduced in this House by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) :
To tlie suitable protection of our exposed coast line and our great sea ports.
-and to the resolution of the government when we say that-
-we are prepared to defend our coast and our shores. [DOT]
If the opinion of the First Lord of the Admiralty is not proper information in matters naval, I must candidly confess, Sir, that I do not know where to seek for better. During the course of the debate, when hon. gentlemen opposite were forced to change front upon this subject, I was reminded very much of the words uttered by an eminent author: ' The human race is divided into classes, those who go ahead and do something, and those who sit back and ask why it is not done the other way.' It seems to me that is about the position: They sit back and say of every proposition in the matter of the construction of a navy, ' Why wasn't it done the other way? ' Let me quote to the House the words of the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden).
Mr. Speaker, I find that it may be some considerable time before I get through the remarks which I propose to make, as I have not entered upon the merits of the Bill, and I propose to discuss the merits. If the House would prefer it, I will move the adjournment of the debate.
